A world in the LEGUIN-EARTHSEA sector, kept after Ursula K. Le Guin — Earthsea.

- Language Magic: a universe where words act directly on reality (fantasy and magical ontologies, extension).
- Exchange Magic: a universe where every intervention exacts a cost (fantasy and magical ontologies, distribution).

sourceText: cells: Tn, Ml, Mx Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the LEGUIN-EARTHSEA sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. True names allow intervention in things, and Aster becomes a threat through her mere capacity to infer them. The memorial bore the name of Ursula K. Le Guin — Earthsea precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Fantasy was introduced not as a suspension of rigor but as a change in the kind of law a world was allowed to admit. A name could have causal force, an oath could become infrastructure, and belief could literally feed a god. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. 301 At the center of the conflict was Sael, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: The children demand that their own deep names remain inaccessible to their creator. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Tn — True Name: a deep name permits intervention upon the thing named; Ml — Language Magic: words act directly on reality; Mx — Exchange Magic: every intervention exacts a cost. Course references included Ursula K. Le Guin — Earthsea; Earthsea; exchange magic. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Vela answered without raising their voice: ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. 302 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS Aster felt the Hunger precisely when an explanation closed too elegantly. A perfect theory reduced surprise, and surprise was the last symptom that something before her had not yet become part of her. The children had noticed that their disagreement calmed her more than any extravagant universe did. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Aster agrees to encode the right in architecture rather than merely promise it. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. The outside residue had become stable enough that Tern could predict where it would not appear: in sectors fully indexed by Aster. He began to believe that the message carried no content at all, but instead demonstrated a boundary — a region in which their instruments received no echo from their own creator. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the SUBSTITUTION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — replaces the substrate, carrier, or medium of a function — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a 303 copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 304 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
